findings.title: `cf config unset` remediation contradicts the design's own delete routing
findings.description:
Line 89 defines delete routing as "mirrors write — deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to" and states `migrate-personal` is "the one exception that touches the *other* project file." For a personal key with `scope: 'project'`, that means `unset git.integration_branch --project` deletes from `.context-forge.local.toml` (the personal file) — it cannot touch the shared file.

Yet the collision-semantics paragraph (line 146) prescribes "a separate, explicit `cf config unset <key> --project`" to clear the *stale shared-file copy*, and Verification Walkthrough step 9 (line 259) requires exactly that and then "confirm `cf check` is clean again." Under the line-89 routing this sequence instead (a) deletes the developer's confirmed personal value — the exact "destroy the developer's local preference" outcome line 146 says must not happen — and (b) leaves the stale shared copy in place, so `cf check` still reports the finding and the walkthrough step fails.

The design must pick one coherent story, e.g.: `unset --project` removes the key from both project files (making line 89's "mirrors write" apply to the primary file plus a documented shared-file cleanup), or the collision remediation becomes "re-run `migrate-personal` after `unset`" / manual edit with the walkthrough updated accordingly. As written, the required migration/compat story's edge-case remediation is broken.

findings.title: `.env.local` analogy oversells the routing semantics
findings.description: The classification rationale (lines 113, 120) justifies the split by pointing at the `.env.local` convention — but in Next.js, `.env.local` overrides *any* variable, whereas this design routes strictly by the key's classification (read step 1 consults the personal file only for `scope === 'personal'` keys). A developer who manually places a shared key (e.g. `workflow.review_enabled`) in `.context-forge.local.toml` gets it silently ignored, with no checker rule or warning (the new `ConsistencyChecker` rule only flags the personal-in-shared direction). Either extend the new rule symmetrically to flag shared-scope keys found in the personal file (cheap, and consistent with the slice's "no silent leak/ignore" goal), or state the ignore behavior explicitly so the analogy doesn't set the wrong expectation.

findings.title: `.gitignore` dedup via substring check can silently skip the needed line
findings.description: The gitignore append uses "a substring/line check." A pure substring test false-positives on near-miss lines (e.g. `.context-forge.local.toml.bak`, or a commented `# .context-forge.local.toml`), causing `cf init` to skip adding the line and leaving the personal file unignored — silently reintroducing the leak this slice exists to prevent. An exact trimmed-line comparison is no more complex than the substring check and eliminates the false-positive direction.

findings.title: Dependency metadata mismatch with the slice plan
findings.description: Plan entry 915 declares "Dependencies: none," while the design lists 914 as a prerequisite and leans on a "916 prerequisite fix (already merged to `main`)" — i.e. work sequenced after this plan entry has already shipped under it. The design's substance is consistent (914 is complete and the plan text itself references `git.integration_branch`), but the plan entry's dependency field should be updated to name 914 so the recorded dependency graph matches reality.
